questions.solution: In each pair the second number is n × (n − 1): 9 × 8 = 72. So 12 × 11 = **132**. (144 = 12² is the trap for those who square.)
questions.shortcut: Test the relation first: 72 = 9 × 8, so the missing value is 12 × 11 = 132.

questions.q: **ABCD : DEFG :: WXYZ : ?**
questions.solution: Each letter moves 3 places forward, wrapping past Z: W→Z, X→A, Y→B, Z→C, giving **ZABC**.
questions.shortcut: W + 3 = Z already pins the answer starting with Z; only two options start with Z, and Z + 3 wraps to A.

questions.q: **Find the odd one out: 361, 441, 484, 512**
questions.solution: 361 = 19², 441 = 21², 484 = 22² are perfect squares, but 512 = 2⁹ is a **perfect cube**, not a square.
questions.shortcut: Scan for squares first (19², 21², 22² are close together); 512 between them breaks the pattern immediately.

questions.q: **Find the next term: 7, 14, 42, 168, 840, ?**
questions.solution: The multipliers grow by 1 each time: ×2 (14), ×3 (42), ×4 (168), ×5 (840), so next is ×6: 840 × 6 = **5040**.
questions.shortcut: Ratios 2, 3, 4, 5 are an arithmetic progression — apply the next ratio directly.

questions.q: **Find the next term: A5B, D10I, G17P, ?**
questions.solution: Three independent patterns: first letters A, D, G, **J** (+3); numbers 5, 10, 17, **26** (gaps +5, +7, +9); last letters B, I, P, **W** (+7). Next term is **J26W**.
questions.shortcut: Treat the three slots separately; the letter gaps (+3, +7) are constant and settle the answer fast.

questions.q: **Find the next term: 2, 3, 8, 27, 112, ?**
questions.shortcut: When growth explodes, check ×1, ×2, ×3… with a small add-on — 112 × 5 + 5 lands on 565.

questions.q: **In a certain code, DELHI is written as CDKGH. How is MUMBAI written in that code?**
questions.solution: Every letter shifts one place back: D→C, E→D, L→K, H→G, I→H. Applying −1 to MUMBAI gives **LTLAZH**.
questions.shortcut: Compare D↔C once — it is a uniform −1 shift; just slide the whole word back.

questions.q: **If RAIN is coded as OJBS, how will GATE be coded in the same language?**
questions.solution: RAIN reversed is NIAR; each letter then moves one forward: OJBS. For GATE: reverse to ETAG, shift +1 → **FUBH**.
questions.shortcut: Check the first code letter: R→O is −3, which is exactly reverse + 1. Apply the same two steps to GATE.

questions.q: **If A = 1, B = 2, …, Z = 26, what is the code of the word HEAD?**
questions.shortcut: Memorise anchor positions (A=1, E=5, H=8, D=4) — the sum is instant.

questions.q: **If '+' means '×', '−' means '+', '×' means '÷' and '÷' means '−', find the value of 8 + 6 − 4 × 2 ÷ 3.**
questions.solution: Replace each operator: 8 × 6 + 4 ÷ 2 − 3. By BODMAS: 48 + 2 − 3 = **47**.
questions.shortcut: Rewrite the full expression once with new signs, then solve left to right respecting ÷/× first.

questions.q: **If '+' and '−' are interchanged, and '×' and '÷' are interchanged, then 12 − 4 + 6 × 3 ÷ 2 = ?**
questions.shortcut: Swap the signs in place first (don't solve as written), then apply BODMAS.

questions.solution: Every row, column and diagonal of this magic square sums to 15. Last column: 6 + 7 + ? = 15 → ? = **2**.
questions.shortcut: Take the completed first row's sum (15) and apply it to the incomplete column.

questions.solution: In every triplet, first − second = third: 12 − 8 = 4, 15 − 9 = 6, 23 − 14 = 9. So 31 − ? = 13 → ? = **18**.
questions.shortcut: Test a − b = c on the first two triplets; once it holds twice, trust it for the third.

questions.q: **Pointing to a man, Meera said, 'He is the son of my grandfather's only son.' How is the man related to Meera?**
questions.solution: Grandfather's only son = Meera's father. The son of Meera's father is Meera's **brother**.
questions.shortcut: 'Only son' collapses the grandfather branch straight to the father — two quick steps, no tree needed.

questions.q: **A is the sister of B. C is the mother of B. D is the father of C. How is A related to D?**
questions.solution: C is mother of B, so C is also mother of A (A is C's daughter). D is father of C, so A is the **granddaughter** of D. A being female (sister of B) fixes the relation as granddaughter, not grandson.
questions.shortcut: Chain the generations: A → daughter of C ← daughter of D, so A is one generation below D.

questions.q: **Ravi walks 5 km towards north, turns right and walks 3 km, turns right again and walks 5 km, then turns left and walks 2 km. How far is he from his starting point?**
questions.solution: Path: north 5 → east 3 → south 5 → east 2. The 5 km north and 5 km south cancel out; net displacement is 3 + 2 = 5 km towards **east**. Shortest distance = **5 km**.
questions.shortcut: The equal north and south legs cancel — only the east legs (3 + 2) survive.

questions.q: **One morning, A and B are talking face to face. A's shadow falls exactly to the left of B. Which direction is B facing?**
questions.solution: In the morning the sun is in the east, so every shadow falls towards the **west**. The shadow lies to B's left, so B's left side is west — which means B is facing **north** (and A faces south).
questions.shortcut: Morning = shadows point west. Map west to the person's left and the facing direction follows.

questions.q: **In a row of 47 students, Ravi is 15th from the left end and Sneha is 9th from the right end. How many students are sitting between them?**
questions.solution: Sneha's position from the left = 47 − 9 + 1 = 39. Students between = 39 − 15 − 1 = **23**.
questions.shortcut: Convert both to the same end, then subtract and drop 1: (47 − 9 + 1) − 15 − 1.

questions.q: **P, Q, R, S, T, U and V sit in a row facing north. Q sits at the extreme left end. U sits at the extreme right end. P is second from the left end. R sits third to the right of P. S sits immediately to the left of R. T sits immediately to the right of P. Who sits exactly in the middle of the row?**
questions.solution:
Fix Q = 1, U = 7, P = 2. R is third to the right of P → R = 5. S immediately left of R → S = 4, and T immediately right of P → T = 3. V takes the remaining seat 6. The middle (4th) seat is **S**.

Row: Q · P · T · S · R · V · U.
questions.shortcut: Lock the two ends and P first; the two 'immediate' clues then fill seats 3 and 4 automatically.

questions.q: **A, B, C, D, E and F sit equally spaced around a circular table, all facing the centre. A sits second to the right of B. C sits immediately to the left of A. E sits opposite B. F is not adjacent to B. Who sits opposite C?**
questions.solution:
Fix B at seat 1 (clockwise numbering 1–6). Facing the centre, 'right' is anticlockwise, so A = 5. 'Left' is clockwise, so C, immediately to A's left, = 6. E opposite B → E = 4. F cannot be next to B, ruling out 2 and 6, so F = 3 and D = 2. Opposite seat 6 (C) is seat 3 — **F**.

Clockwise: B · D · F · E · A · C.
questions.shortcut: For centre-facing circles remember: right = anticlockwise, left = clockwise. Fix one person and place everyone relative to them.

questions.q: **M, N, O, P, Q and R sit in a row facing south. P sits fourth to the left of M. N sits between M and P. Q sits at one of the extreme ends. R sits immediately to the right of N. O does not sit at any extreme end. How many people sit between Q and P?**
questions.solution:
Facing south, a person's left is the right side of the row as drawn, so positions flip. P fourth to the left of M forces M = 2 and P = 6 (only arrangement inside a 6-seat row). N between M and P, with R immediately to the right of N (right = lower seat number when facing south): N = 4, R = 3. O takes 5, and Q takes the end seat 1.

Row (as drawn): Q · M · R · N · O · P. Between Q (1) and P (6) sit M, R, N, O = **4** people.
questions.shortcut: For south-facing rows, swap every 'left' and 'right' clue before placing people; then count the gap directly.

questions.q:
**Statements: All pens are clocks. Some clocks are mirrors. All mirrors are books.**

**Conclusions:** I. Some books are pens. II. Some books are clocks.
questions.solution: II follows directly: some clocks are mirrors and all mirrors are books, so those clocks are books — some books are clocks. I does not follow: the clocks that are pens may not overlap the clocks that are mirrors, so no book need be a pen.
questions.shortcut: Chain only the statements that share a term. Pens never connect to mirrors, so any book–pen claim fails.

questions.q:
**Statements: No apple is a banana. All bananas are mangoes.**

**Conclusions:** I. Some mangoes are not apples. II. All mangoes are bananas.
questions.solution: All bananas are mangoes, and no banana is an apple — so the mangoes that are bananas are definitely not apples: some mangoes are not apples. I follows. II reverses 'all bananas are mangoes', which is invalid.
questions.shortcut: 'All A are B' never converts to 'all B are A' — that alone kills II; verify I by chaining bananas → mangoes.

questions.q: **In a group of 80 students, 40 play cricket, 35 play football and 30 play hockey. 15 play cricket and football, 12 play football and hockey, 10 play cricket and hockey, and 5 play all three games. How many students play none of the three games?**
questions.solution: n(at least one) = 40 + 35 + 30 − 15 − 12 − 10 + 5 = **73**. Playing none = 80 − 73 = **7**. (Add the all-three count back — subtracting the pairwise overlaps removed it three times but it should stay once.)
questions.shortcut: Three-set formula in one line: sum of singles − sum of pairs + all-three, then subtract from the total.

questions.q:
**Arrange the following words as they would appear in an English dictionary:**

1. Rigid  2. Ribbon  3. Ridicule  4. Rifle  5. Rigour
questions.solution: Compare letter by letter: Ribbon (Rib**b**) < Ridicule (Rid) < Rifle (Rif) < Rigid (Rig**i**) < Rigour (Rig**o**), since b < d < f < g and i < o. Order: **2, 3, 4, 1, 5**.
questions.shortcut: Sort by the third letter first (b, d, f, g, g); only the two Rig- words need the fourth letter to separate.

questions.q:
**Statement: 'All students must submit their assignments by Friday. Late submissions will not be accepted.' — circular issued by the college**

**Conclusions:** I. A student who submits the assignment on Saturday will not have it accepted. II. Some students may have already submitted their assignments.
questions.solution: I follows directly from the notice: Saturday is after Friday, so the submission will not be accepted. II is only a possibility — the statement says nothing about what has already happened — so it is not a definite conclusion.
questions.shortcut: Possibility ('may have') is never a valid conclusion in statement–conclusion questions unless the statement implies it.

questions.q: **How many triangles are there in the figure below?**
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 160 92" width="160" height="92" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><polygon points="80,8 12,84 148,84"/><line x1="80" y1="8" x2="57" y2="84"/><line x1="80" y1="8" x2="103" y2="84"/></svg>
questions.solution: Two cevians divide the base into 3 parts, giving 3 small triangles. Triangles formed by joining 2 adjacent parts: 2. The whole triangle: 1. Total = 3 + 2 + 1 = **6**.
questions.shortcut: With n cevians from one apex to the base, triangles = (n+1)(n+2)/2. Here n = 2 → 6.

questions.q: **Which of the following words will appear exactly the same when seen in a mirror placed vertically beside it?**
questions.solution: A vertical mirror flips each letter horizontally. M and O are symmetric left–right, so MOM reads the same. In NOON the N becomes И; in POOL the P and L flip; in SUN the S, U and N all change.
questions.shortcut: Check each letter for left–right symmetry (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y); one asymmetric letter kills the word.

questions.q: **A square sheet of paper is folded once vertically and then once horizontally, as shown. A single hole is then punched in the middle of the folded sheet. How many holes will the fully unfolded sheet have?**
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 190 100" width="190" height="100" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><rect x="12" y="12" width="76" height="76" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="50" y1="12" x2="50" y2="88" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/><line x1="12" y1="50" x2="88" y2="50" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/><line x1="60" y1="26" x2="74" y2="26"/><polyline points="69.5,21.5 74,26 69.5,30.5"/><line x1="26" y1="36" x2="26" y2="50"/><polyline points="21.5,45.5 26,50 30.5,45.5"/><rect x="128" y="26" width="40" height="40"/><circle cx="148" cy="46" r="4.5" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></svg>
questions.solution: Two folds make 4 layers (2 × 2). One punch passes through all 4 layers, and unfolding mirrors the hole across both fold lines, so the sheet shows 2 × 2 = **4** holes arranged in a small square around the centre.
questions.shortcut: Holes = layers at the punch point. Each fold doubles the layers; two folds → 4.

questions.q: **A dice shows 3, 4 and 6 on its visible faces in one view, and 1, 4 and 6 in another view of the same dice (4 and 6 in the same relative position in both views). Which number is on the face opposite 3?**
questions.solution: Faces 4 and 6 are common to both views and keep the same relative position, so the remaining faces of the two views must be opposite each other: **3 is opposite 1** (and by elimination 2 is opposite 5).
questions.shortcut: Two views sharing two faces in the same orientation → the odd faces out are opposite each other.
